units.title: Hello, C#
units.summary: Write your first C# program and print text and numbers with `Console.WriteLine`.

lesson.md: A C# program is a list of **statements**. The computer runs them from top to bottom. Your first statement prints a line of text with `Console.WriteLine`.

lesson.code: Console.WriteLine("Hello, World!");

lesson.md: Text in double quotes, like `"Hello"`, is called a **string**. Every statement ends with a semicolon `;`. If you forget it, the program does not compile.

This one line is already a complete program. Modern C# lets you write statements directly in the file, without any extra structure around them. They are called **top-level statements**. A new project from `dotnet new console` starts exactly like this.
Numbers are written without quotes. C# can calculate with them: `+` adds, `-` subtracts, `*` multiplies and `/` divides.
C# follows the usual math rules: `*` and `/` come before `+` and `-`. Parentheses `( )` make C# calculate a part first. A calculation in quotes is only text, so `"2 + 3"` prints as it is.
`Console.Write` prints text without starting a new line afterwards. `Console.WriteLine()` with nothing inside the parentheses only ends the current line.
C# is case-sensitive. `Console.WriteLine` works, but `console.writeline` does not compile.

card: `"text"` is a string, `42` is a number

exercises.explain: C# is case-sensitive, and text must be in double quotes. The method is `Console.WriteLine`.

exercises.code: Console.WriteLine(3 + 4 * 2);
exercises.explain: `*` comes before `+`: first `4 * 2` is `8`, then `3 + 8` is `11`.
The semicolon is missing. Every statement in C# ends with `;`.

exercises.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints `Hello` and `World` on two separate lines.
exercises.code:
Console.___("Hello");
Console.WriteLine("World");
exercises.explain: `WriteLine` ends the line after `Hello`. `Write` would print `HelloWorld` on one line, and `Print` does not exist.
`Console.Write` does not start a new line, so `A`, `B` and `C` end up on the same line.
The last line has no semicolon. Write `Console.WriteLine("C#");`.

exercises.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `Hi, Ana!` and then `Bye`.
exercises.explain: `Console.Write` keeps the first three parts on one line. `WriteLine("!")` ends that line, so `Bye` comes on the next one.

exercises.prompt: Build a line that prints the result of `6 * 7`.
exercises.explain: Numbers without quotes are calculated, so the line prints `42`. With quotes, it would print the text `6 * 7`.

exercises.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.

prints x without a line break

exercises.code: Console.WriteLine("10 + 5");
exercises.explain: The calculation is inside double quotes, so it is a string. C# prints the text exactly as it is.

exercises.code: Console.WriteLine((2 + 3) * 4);
exercises.explain: The parentheses come first: `2 + 3` is `5`, and `5 * 4` is `20`.

exercises.statement: `Console.Write` starts a new line after the text.
exercises.explain: Only `Console.WriteLine` ends the line. `Console.Write("A")` followed by `Console.Write("B")` prints `AB`.

units.title: Variables and types
units.summary: Store values in variables and get to know `int`, `double`, `string`, `bool`, `char`, `var` and `const`.

lesson.md: A **variable** is a named box for a value. You create it with a type, a name, `=` and a value. After that, you use the name instead of the value. Variable names usually start with a small letter, like `age` or `firstName`.
You can give a variable a new value later. The old value is then gone. You write the type only once, when you create the variable.

Every variable has a **type** that never changes. `int` holds whole numbers, `double` holds numbers with a decimal point, `string` holds text, `bool` holds `true` or `false`, and `char` holds a single character in single quotes.
`Console.WriteLine` prints a `bool` as `True` or `False` with a capital letter. In code, you always write `true` and `false`.
A variable cannot change its type. `int count = "three";` does not compile, because `"three"` is a `string`, not an `int`.
With `var`, C# works out the type from the value. `var total = 12;` creates an `int`. The type is still fixed: you cannot store text in `total` later.
A `const` is a value that never changes. Giving `MaxPlayers` a new value is an error. Names of constants usually start with a capital letter.
On some computers, a `double` prints with a comma instead of a point, for example `4,5` instead of `4.5`. This depends on the language settings of the system.

card: `var x = 5;` lets C# find the type

exercises.prompt: Match each type with what it holds.
pairs: a number with a decimal point

exercises.explain: `x` starts at `5`. Then `5 + 3` is `8`, and `8 * 2` is `16`.

exercises.prompt: Which line creates a variable that holds a single character?
exercises.explain: A `char` value is written in single quotes. Double quotes make a `string`, and `x` without quotes is a name, not a value.

n = "ten";
exercises.explain: `var n = 10;` makes `n` an `int`, and the type never changes. Storing `"ten"` in it is an error.

exercises.explain: `2.5` has a decimal point, so the type is `double`. An `int` cannot hold `2.5`.
`b = a` copies the value `"Hi"` into `b`. Changing `a` later does not change `b`.
`Days` is a `const`, so you cannot give it a new value. Remove the line `Days = 8;`.

exercises.explain: `Console.WriteLine` prints a `bool` with a capital letter: `False`.

exercises.explain: First the type, then the name, then `=` and the value. Text goes in double quotes.

exercises.explain: A variable must exist before you use it: `height` needs `width`, `area` needs both, and the output comes last.
`*` comes first: `Step * 3` is `6`, and `7 - 6` is `1`.
In code you write `true`, but `Console.WriteLine` prints a `bool` with a capital letter.

units.title: Strings and operators
units.summary: Join and format text, use string methods like `ToUpper` and `Substring`, and calculate with `%`, `+=` and `++`.

lesson.md: You can join two strings with `+`. This is called **concatenation**. A number joined with a string becomes text too.

A string that starts with `$` can contain values in curly braces, like `$"Hi, {name}!"`. This is called **string interpolation**, and it is often easier to read than `+`. You can also put calculations inside the braces.

`Length` tells you how many characters a string has. `ToUpper()` and `ToLower()` give you the text in capital or small letters. `Substring(start, length)` gives you a part of the string. Positions start at `0`, not at `1`.

`Substring(3)` without a length gives you everything from position `3` to the end. `word[0]` gives you the first character as a `char`. Methods like `ToUpper()` never change the original string. They return a new one.

Besides `+`, `-`, `*` and `/`, there is `%`: the remainder of a division. When you divide two `int` values, the result is an `int` too, and the part after the decimal point is cut off. Use a `double` like `7.0` to keep it.
`x += 5` is short for `x = x + 5`. The same works with `-=`, `*=` and `/=`. `x++` adds `1` to `x`, and `x--` subtracts `1`.
`+` with a string and a number joins them as text. `"1" + 2` gives `"12"`, not `3`.

exercises.code:
string s = "Hello";
Console.WriteLine(s.Length);
exercises.explain: `Length` counts the characters: `H`, `e`, `l`, `l`, `o`.

exercises.code: Console.WriteLine(17 % 5);
exercises.explain: `17 / 5` is `3` with a remainder of `2`, and `%` gives the remainder.

exercises.code: Console.WriteLine("1" + 2);
exercises.explain: `"1"` is a string, so `+` joins the text `"1"` and `2` to `"12"`.

exercises.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints `Hi, Lea!`.
exercises.code:

Console.WriteLine(___"Hi, {name}!");
exercises.explain: Only a string that starts with `$` replaces `{name}` with the value of `name`.

exercises.prompt: Build a line that prints the first 3 characters of `text`.
exercises.explain: `Substring(0, 3)` starts at position `0` and takes `3` characters.
`ToUpper()` returns a new string, but the program does not store it. `s` is still `"cat"`.

exercises.prompt: The program should print `Rome in 2025`. Which line has the bug?
exercises.explain: The `$` is missing, so the braces are printed as normal text. Write `$"{city} in {year}"`.
`x *= 3` makes `x` `12`, and `x--` subtracts `1`, so it is `11`.

exercises.prompt: What is the value of `10 / 4` in C#?
exercises.explain: Both numbers are `int`, so the result is an `int`. The part after the decimal point is cut off.

exercises.explain: Each line uses the variable from the line before it, so this is the only order that works.

exercises.explain: Positions start at `0`: `P` is at `0`, `l` at `1` and `a` at `2`.

units.title: Decisions
units.summary: Let your program choose with `if` and `else`, compare values, combine conditions and use switch expressions.

lesson.md: Programs often need to make a choice. An `if` statement runs a block of code only when its condition is `true`. The block is written in curly braces `{ }`.
With `else`, you say what happens when the condition is `false`. With `else if`, you check more conditions one after another. C# runs the first block whose condition is `true` and skips the rest.

A comparison gives a `bool`. The operators are `==` (equal), `!=` (not equal), `<` (less than), `>` (greater than), `<=` (less or equal) and `>=` (greater or equal). You can compare strings with `==` too.
`=` gives a variable a value, `==` compares two values. `if (a = 5)` does not compile in C#.
You can combine conditions: `&&` means and (both must be `true`), `||` means or (at least one must be `true`), and `!` means not (it turns `true` into `false` and the other way round).

A **switch expression** picks one result out of several cases. Each case has the form `value => result`, and the cases are separated by commas. The underscore `_` matches every other value, like a final `else`.

exercises.explain: `7 > 10` is `false`, so the `else` block runs.
C# runs only the first block whose condition is `true`. `15 > 5` is already `true`, so the other branches are skipped.
`&&` needs both sides to be `true`. `b` is `false`, so the result is `False`.

exercises.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints `Equal`.
exercises.explain: `==` compares two values. A single `=` assigns a value and does not compile inside `if`.
`else` never has a condition. Write only `else`, or use `else if (age < 18)`.

exercises.prompt: Match the operator with its meaning.

exercises.explain: `size` is `"M"`, so the case `"M" => 7` matches.

exercises.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `Even`.
exercises.explain: Each variable needs the one before it. In the switch expression, `_` must be the last case, because it matches every value.

exercises.prompt: Build the line that checks that `age` is at least `18` and `member` is `true`.
exercises.explain: `>=` means greater or equal, and `&&` needs both conditions to be `true`.
`||` is `true` when at least one side is `true`. `&&` means and, `!` means not.

exercises.statement: In a switch expression, `_` matches every value that no other case matched.
exercises.explain: `_` is the discard pattern. It works like a final `else`.
`a > b` is `false`, so `!(a > b)` is `true`. But `b != 8` is `false`, and `true && false` is `False`.

units.title: Loops
units.summary: Repeat code with `for`, `while` and `foreach`, and control a loop with `break` and `continue`.

lesson.md: A **loop** repeats code. The `for` loop is the classic way to count. It has three parts in parentheses, separated by semicolons: a start, a condition and a step.

`int i = 1` runs once at the start. Before each round, C# checks `i <= 3`. After each round, `i++` adds `1` to `i`. As soon as the condition is `false`, the loop ends. A loop is also useful to add up numbers.

A `while` loop repeats its block as long as the condition is `true`. Use it when you do not know in advance how many rounds you need. Make sure the condition becomes `false` at some point, or the loop never ends.
A `foreach` loop goes through every item of a collection, one after another. A string is a collection of characters, so you can loop over it. You meet more collections in a later world.
`break` ends the whole loop at once. `continue` skips the rest of the current round and goes on with the next round.
To count down, start high and use `i--`. The loop `for (int i = 3; i > 0; i--)` counts `3`, `2`, `1`.

card: `break` ends the loop, `continue` skips one round

exercises.explain: `i` starts at `0` and the loop runs while `i < 4`, so it prints `0`, `1`, `2` and `3` on one line.
`i` takes the values `2`, `4` and `6`. Their sum is `12`.

units.title: Methods
units.summary: Write your own methods with parameters, return values and optional parameters, and call them as often as you need.

lesson.md: A **method** is a named block of code that you can run as often as you want. You already use methods like `Console.WriteLine`. Now you write your own.

`void` means that the method gives nothing back. The name is followed by parentheses, and method names in C# start with a capital letter. To run a method, you **call** it: write its name with parentheses.

**Parameters** are inputs of a method. Each parameter has a type and a name. When you call the method, you pass a value for each parameter, called an **argument**. Inside the method, the parameter is a new variable with a copy of that value.

lesson.output:
Hi, Zoe!
Hi, Zoe!
Hi, Tom!

lesson.md: A method can calculate a value and give it back with `return`. Instead of `void`, you write the type of the result before the name. `return` also ends the method at once.
If a method only returns one expression, you can use the short form with `=>`. The method `IsEven` below returns a `bool`.

A parameter with a default value is **optional**. If you leave out the argument, C# uses the default. You can also write the name of a parameter in the call, like `count: 2`. Then the order of the arguments does not matter.

lesson.output:
1 x pen
3 x cup
2 x book

lesson.md: Here the methods live directly in the program file, next to the top-level statements. Methods inside a class, which you meet in the last world, work the same way.

units.title: Arrays and lists
units.summary: Store many values in arrays, lists and dictionaries, and go through them with `foreach`.

lesson.md: An **array** stores several values of the same type in one variable. You write the type with square brackets, like `int[]`, and the values in `[ ]`. Each value has a position, the **index**, which starts at `0`.
The last index is `Length - 1`. Reading `scores[3]` from an array with three items stops the program with an `IndexOutOfRangeException`.

An array has a fixed size. A `List<T>` can grow and shrink. `T` stands for the type of the items, so `List<string>` is a list of strings. `Add` adds an item at the end, `Remove` deletes one, and `Count` tells you how many items there are.
`foreach` goes through all items of an array or a list. To print all items on one line, use `string.Join` with a separator.
`Console.WriteLine(numbers)` does not print the items, only the name of the type. Use `string.Join` or a loop instead.
A `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>` stores pairs of a **key** and a **value**. You look up a value by its key, like a word in a dictionary. Each key exists only once.

`new Dictionary<string, int>()` creates an empty dictionary with `string` keys and `int` values. Assigning to `ages["Ana"]` again replaces the old value. Reading a key that does not exist stops the program, so check it with `ContainsKey` first.

exercises.code:
int[] a = [4, 7, 1, 9];
Console.WriteLine(a[2]);
exercises.explain: The index starts at `0`: `a[0]` is `4`, `a[1]` is `7` and `a[2]` is `1`.
The list starts with two names, gets two more and loses one: `2 + 2 - 1` is `3`.

exercises.prompt: Which index does the first item of an array have?
exercises.explain: In C#, counting positions starts at `0`. The second item has the index `1`.

exercises.explain: An array has a fixed size and no `Add` method. Use a `List<int>` if you need to add items.

units.title: Classes and objects
units.summary: Define your own types with classes, properties, constructors and methods, and store data with records.

lesson.md: A **class** is a blueprint for your own type. It bundles data and the methods that work with that data. An **object** is one concrete thing that you build from a class with `new`.

`Name` and `Age` are **properties**: values that every object of the class has. `{ get; set; }` means you can read and change them, and `public` means code outside the class can use them. `= ""` gives `Name` an empty text as start value. In a program with top-level statements, classes go at the end of the file.
A **constructor** runs when you create an object with `new`. It has the same name as the class and no return type. Use it to give the properties their start values.
A property with only `get` can be set in the constructor, but not changed later. This protects the data of an object from mistakes.

A class can have methods that use the properties of the object. Each object keeps its own values, so the same method changes only the object you call it on. `private set` means that only code inside the class can change `Value`.

A **record** is a short way to define a type that mainly holds data. One line creates the properties and the constructor. Records also print their values in a readable way, and two records with the same values are equal.
Two objects of a normal class are only equal with `==` if they are the very same object. Use a record when you want to compare the values.

card: `class Dog { public string Name { get; set; } = ""; }`
`var d = new Dog();` creates an object
`public Dog(string name) { Name = name; }` is a constructor
`record Point(int X, int Y);` is a data type
Classes go after the top-level statements
